items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: Phil Schaap is mentioned only in a parenthetical note by the interviewer/editor; the interviewee Harry Edison does not speak about Phil Schaap.

ctx.x: Bobby Moore, yeah. Bobby Moore. Yeah, I was thinking about another trumpet player. It was Bobby Moore.

*Rust's Jazz Records lists the following succession of trumpeters for the 1937-38 Basie band: Bobby Moore, Bobby Hicks, Karl Georne, and for a recording on February 16, 1938, Harry Edison. Phil Schaap believes Hicks is a pseudonym.

He had trouble with his teeth or something, you know. And he was a good trumpet player. He was a fantastic trumpet player, geemanetti, he could play. And when he took ill, Herschel -- we were all staying at the same rooming house, Herschel Evans, Jo Jones, Page said, why don't you get Harry, you know. And in fact, Lucky had fired me for Dizzy. He fired me for Dizzy Gillespie. And because --

items.title: Phil Schaap interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003
items.q: I knew Sweets well and he always was sweet to me.

ctx.x: My name is Monk Rowe and we are in Toronto for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive. I’m extremely pleased to have Phil Schaap with me here. I’m just going to call you a keeper of the jazz flame, and we can talk about the things you’ve done. You were just talking about, before the cameras were rolling, your teachers. And you mentioned Basie alumnus.

Yeah, well alumni actually, Jo Jones, who the only people who called him Papa Jo Jones when I met him were his children, and some of them were pretty young. A couple of them were not born yet. And he was significantly younger than I am now. I am 51 and he was 44. That’s significant. And Earle Warren, the leader of the reeds. I mean I don’t know whether it was coincidence or because of their camaraderie, which once I intersected with it facilitated more Basieites being involved with the nurturing of me as a child…
